messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Non-linear regression: odd model behaviour
parts:
Dear Stan Developers,

First of all, thanks for making my life easier! I really appreciate how the Stan language forces me to properly write up a model. With BUGS, I was always debugging my models for what seems like ages, which is no longer the case with Stan.

I would like to pose a question about non-linear model behaviour. I'm working on a hierarchical model for blood parasite levels in experimentally infected subjects, assuming a log-normal distribution for blood parasite levels. The blood parasites appear in cycles of generations, each cycle being modeled by two scaled normal cdf's (one for the build-up of parasites, another for the disappearing of parasites). To anchor the model, I'm explicitly modeling censored observations, and I assume that all observations up to the first observation above the detection limit are samples of first generation of blood parasites.

data {
  int<lower=1> Nobs;                                // Number of observations;
  int<lower=1> Nind;                                // Number of individuals;
  int<lower=1> Nobs_ind[Nind];                      // Number of observations in each individual;
  int<lower=1> Ncyc;                                // Number of cycles to model;
 
  int<lower=1> N_cens1;                             // Number of censored observations before first positive observation;
  int<lower=1> id_cens1[N_cens1];                   // Individual to which censored observation pertains;
  real<lower=0> time_cens1[N_cens1];                // Time of censored observation;
  real<lower=0> dlimit_cens1[N_cens1];              // Lower detection limit of blood parasite concentrations;
 
  int<lower=1> N_cens2;                             // Number of censored observations after first positive observation;
  int<lower=1> id_cens2[N_cens2];                   // Individual to which censored observation pertains;
  real<lower=0> time_cens2[N_cens2];                // Time of censored observation;
  real<lower=0> dlimit_cens2[N_cens2];              // Lower detection limit of blood parasite concentrations;
 
  int<lower=1> N_firstpos;                          // Number of first positive observations;
  int<lower=1> id_firstpos[N_firstpos];             // Individual to which first positive observation pertains;
  real<lower=0> time_firstpos[N_firstpos];          // Time of first positive observation;
  real<lower=0> pf_ml_firstpos[N_firstpos];         // Value of first positive observation;
 
  int<lower=1> N_cyc1plus;                          // Number of non-censored observations after first positive observation;
  int<lower=1> id_cyc1plus[N_cyc1plus];             // Individual to which non-censored observation after first positive observation pertains;
  real<lower=0> time_cyc1plus[N_cyc1plus];          // Time of non-censored observation after first positive observation;
  real<lower=0> pf_ml_cyc1plus[N_cyc1plus];         // Value of non-censored observation after first positive observation;
 
  real<lower=0> s2;                                 // Standard deviation (within individuals) of time of disappearance of parasites (currently set to zero);
  real<lower=0> s3;                                 // Standard deviation (within individuals) of duration of undetectable parasite form (currentlyset to zero);
  real<lower=0> constant;                           // Small constant to add to modeled parasite blood concentration for numerical stability;
}
parameters {
  real log_T1;                                      // Log average time of appearance of parasites in the population;
  real<lower=5,upper=12> t1[Nind];                  // Average time of appearance of parasites in individuals;
  real<lower=0,upper=10> S_T1;                      // Standard deviation (between individuals) of time of appearance of parasites;
  real<lower=0> s1;                                 // Standard deviation (within individuals) of time of appearance of parasites;
 
  real<lower=0,upper=4> t23;                        // Parasite generation time;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> t2of3;                      // Fraction of parasite generation time spent in detectable form;
 
  real log_M1;                                      // Log average number of parasites per ml blood during first cycle in the population;
  real<lower=0> m1[Nind];                           // Number of parasites per ml during first cycle in individuals;
  real<lower=0,upper=10> S_M1;                      // Standard deviation (between individuals) of average number of parasites per ml during first cycle;
 
  real<lower=0> log_R;                              // Log average number of new parasites per parasite from previous cycle in population;
  real<lower=1> r[Nind];                            // Number of new parasites per ringform from previous cycle in individuals;
  real<lower=0,upper=10> S_R;                       // Standard deviation (between individuals) of log number of new parasites per parasite from previous cycle;
 
  real<lower=0,upper=10> sigma;                     // Standard deviation of measurement error in log-concentration of parasites;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> t2;                                 // Duration of detectable parasite form;
  real<lower=0> t3;                                 // Duration of undetectable parasite form;
  real<lower=1> R;                                    // Average number of parasites per ml blood during first cycle in the population;
 
  t2 <- t23 * t2of3;
  t3 <- t23 * (1 - t2of3);
  R <- exp(log_R);
}
model {
  real PF_ML_CENS1[N_cens1];                        // True value of censored observations before first positives;
  real PF_ML_CENS2[N_cens2,Ncyc];                   // True value of censored observations after first positives;
  real PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[N_firstpos];                  // True value of first positive observations;
  real PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[N_cyc1plus,Ncyc];             // True value of positive observations after the first positive observation;
 
  real log_PF_ML_CENS1[N_cens1];                    // Log true value of censored observations before first positives;
  real log_PF_ML_CENS2[N_cens2];                    // Log true value of censored observations after first positives;
  real log_PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[N_firstpos];              // Log true value of first positive observations;
  real log_PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[N_cyc1plus];              // Log true value of positive observations after the first positive observation;

  t1 ~ lognormal(log_T1,S_T1);
  m1 ~ lognormal(log_M1,S_M1);
  r ~ lognormal(log_R,S_R);   

  for (c in 1:N_cens1) {
    PF_ML_CENS1[c] <- constant +
        m1[id_cens1[c]]
        * (normal_cdf( time_cens1[c],  t1[id_cens1[c]]      , s1 )
        -  normal_cdf( time_cens1[c], (t1[id_cens1[c]] + t2), sqrt(s1*s1 + s2*s2) ));
    log_PF_ML_CENS1[c] <- log(PF_ML_CENS1[c]);
  }
 
  for(cc in 1:N_cens2) {
    for(k in 1:Ncyc) {
      PF_ML_CENS2[cc,k] <- constant +
          m1[id_cens2[cc]] * pow(r[id_cens2[cc]],(k-1))
          * (normal_cdf( time_cens2[cc], (t1[id_cens2[cc]] + (k-1) * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 + (k-1) * s2*s2 + (k-1) * s3*s3) )
          -  normal_cdf( time_cens2[cc], (t1[id_cens2[cc]] +     k * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 +     k * s2*s2 + (k-1) * s3*s3) ));
    }
  log_PF_ML_CENS2[cc] <- log(sum(PF_ML_CENS2[cc]));
  }

  for(f in 1:N_firstpos) {
    PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[f] <- constant +
        m1[id_firstpos[f]]
        * (normal_cdf( time_firstpos[f],  t1[id_firstpos[f]]      , s1 )
        -  normal_cdf( time_firstpos[f], (t1[id_firstpos[f]] + t2), sqrt(s1*s1 + s2*s2) ));
    log_PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[f] <- log(PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[f]);
  }
 
  for(p in 1:N_cyc1plus) {
    for(k in 1:Ncyc) {
      PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[p,k] <- constant +
          m1[id_cyc1plus[p]] * pow(r[id_cyc1plus[p]],(k-1))
          * (normal_cdf( time_cyc1plus[p], (t1[id_cyc1plus[p]] + (k-1) * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 + (k-1) * s2*s2 + (k-1) * s3*s3) )
          -  normal_cdf( time_cyc1plus[p], (t1[id_cyc1plus[p]] +     k * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 +     k * s2*s2 + (k-1) * s3*s3) ));
    }
  log_PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[p] <- log(sum(PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[p]));
  }

  for (c in 1:N_cens1) {
    lp__ <- lp__ + log(lognormal_cdf(log(dlimit_cens1[c]),log_PF_ML_CENS1[c],sigma));     // Integrate out censored value;
  }
  for (cc in 1:N_cens2) {
    lp__ <- lp__ + log(lognormal_cdf(log(dlimit_cens2[cc]),log_PF_ML_CENS2[cc],sigma));   // Integrate out censored value;
  }
  pf_ml_firstpos ~ lognormal(log_PF_ML_FIRSTPOS,sigma);
  pf_ml_cyc1plus ~ lognormal(log_PF_ML_CYC1PLUS,sigma);
}

My model is compiling nicely, and comes up with very plausible parameter estimates. Also, visually, the model predictions fit the data well (see attached example). However, when looking at the traceplots, it seems that the model sometimes gets 'spontaneously' stuck at a set of parameter values for some hundreds of MC simulations at a time (coinciding with a high lp, and with all of the parameters having plausible values, no zeros or infinities etc). In general, N.eff is very low. Is there a way to get this (or any model) explore local maxima/minima more efficiently? I have tried to leave out the hierarchical components for parameter R (number of new parasites per parasite), which considerably improved mixing of chains (and I haven't noticed the sampler getting stuck when doing this). Still, I'm interested to know whether it is possible to further improve sampling efficiency.

Thanks in advance for any pointers!

Luc

On 3/17/13 4:46 AM, Luc Coffeng wrote:
> Dear Stan Developers,
>
> First of all, thanks for making my life easier! I really appreciate how the Stan language forces me to properly write up
> a model. With BUGS, I was always debugging my models for what seems like ages, which is no longer the case with Stan.

Glad you appreciate it -- I like the typing
and declaration of variables because it's where
I usually make mistakes when coding. Opinions vary
on how far to go with this kind of thing.

To answer the question below about efficient mixing in hierarchical
models, I have three suggestions, none of which are specific
to your model.

First, check to make sure the log probability function has support
on the entire parameter space as determined by the constraint declarations.
For instance, if you declare something as y<lower=6,upper=12>, it
needs to be valid to have y be anywhere between 6 and 12.
If not, you can wind up near a constraint boundary
and find random movements leading to illegal values, which
are always rejected, so it just looks like the chain's not moving.
This shouldn't happen if the log probability function has support
on the parameters as declared. Sometimes this can take some
mental wrangling, because we don't have a super expressive constraint
language. In extreme cases, you may have to define your own
transforms and Jacobians.

Second, I'd suggest reading the manual section on optimization
and reparameterization. The funnel example is an extreme example
of what can go wrong with hierarchical models and how to
reparameterize them for more efficient sampling (in terms of
effective samples per iteration). You may have some mental gymnastics
to deal with the lognormal distribution.

Third, the halfway point between fixing the priors and setting
them free is to give them informative priors.

In terms of code efficiency (time per iteration, not effective
samples per iteration), there are a couple things you can do and
a couple things we have in the works that'll make these models faster
in the future as written.

Unlike BUGS, Stan lets you reset local variables like local variables.
So your loop:

> for(cc in 1:N_cens2) {
> for(k in 1:Ncyc) {
> PF_ML_CENS2[cc,k] <- constant +
> m1[id_cens2[cc]] * pow(r[id_cens2[cc]],(k-1))
> * (normal_cdf( time_cens2[cc], (t1[id_cens2[cc]] + (k-1) * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 + (k-1) * s2*s2 +
> (k-1) * s3*s3) )
> - normal_cdf( time_cens2[cc], (t1[id_cens2[cc]] + k * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 + k * s2*s2 +
> (k-1) * s3*s3) ));
> }
> log_PF_ML_CENS2[cc] <- log(sum(PF_ML_CENS2[cc]));
> }
could be reimplemented as:
for (cc in 1:N_cens2) {

sum <- 0;
for (k in 1:Ncyc)
sum <- sum + [constant + ....];
log_PF_ML_CENS2[cc] <- log(sum);
}

It probably won't be noticeably faster, but it will take up
less memory.

We haven't come close to speeding up all the
truncated and censored models that we could. The first step is
to properly vectorize all the cdfs -- we're about to do normal.
The second step is integrating with the pdfs more closely to
remove redundant calculations. When we implement Riemann-manifold
HMC later this year, it should take care of all these mixing problems
at the expense of each iteration being slower.

I hope that's clear -- if not, we can help with some of
the reparameterizations.

- Bob

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Non-linear regression: odd model behaviour
parts:
Thanks Bob for the tips and for reminding me about the support of the log probability function. I guess I should truncate some of the priors/hyperparameters declared in the model{} statement.

I have been trying to reparameterize the log-normal distribution in terms of a unit log-normal distribution and separate mean and scale terms (after the example of the normal distribution in the manual). And yes, that's proper mind gymnastics, so for anyone else who is looking to reparameterize the lognormal distribution, here's what I tried:

x ~ lognormal(mu_log,sigma)

is equal to

x.raw ~ lognormal(0,1)
x <- exp(mu_log + log(x.raw)*sigma)

or

x.raw ~ normal(0,1)
x <- exp(mu_log + x.raw*sigma)

I'm not quite sure whether the last reparameterization also requires me also to specify the Jacobian of the transform, so perhaps someone can comment on this. This Jacobian stuff is really beyond me (I'm not a statistician or mathematician). I abandonned the approach altogether when the model went completely berserk. May give it another try later, once I have solved the other issues pointed out by Bob.

Best,
Luc

 > (k-1) * s3*s3) )
 >            -  normal_cdf( time_cens2[cc], (t1[id_cens2[cc]] +     k * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 +     k * s2*s2 +
 > (k-1) * s3*s3) ));
 >      }
 >    log_PF_ML_CENS2[cc] <- log(sum(PF_ML_CENS2[cc]));
 >    }

could be reimplemented as:

   for (cc in 1:N_cens2) {
     sum <- 0;
     for (k in 1:Ncyc)
       sum <- sum + [constant + ....];
     log_PF_ML_CENS2[cc] <- log(sum);
   }

It probably won't be noticeably faster, but it will take up
less memory.

We haven't come close to speeding up all the
truncated and censored models that we could.  The first step is
to properly vectorize all the cdfs -- we're about to do normal.
The second step is integrating with the pdfs more closely to
remove redundant calculations.  When we implement Riemann-manifold
HMC later this year, it should take care of all these mixing problems
at the expense of each iteration being slower.

I hope that's clear -- if not, we can help with some of
the reparameterizations.

- Bob

On 3/18/13 4:20 AM, Luc Coffeng wrote:
> Thanks Bob for the tips and for reminding me about the support of the log probability function. I guess I should
> truncate some of the priors/hyperparameters declared in the model{} statement.
>
> I have been trying to reparameterize the log-normal distribution in terms of a unit log-normal distribution and separate
> mean and scale terms (after the example of the normal distribution in the manual). And yes, that's proper mind
> gymnastics, so for anyone else who is looking to reparameterize the lognormal distribution, here's what I tried:
>
> x ~ lognormal(mu_log,sigma)
>
> is equal to
>
> x.raw ~ lognormal(0,1)
> x <- exp(mu_log + log(x.raw)*sigma)
>
> or
>
> x.raw ~ normal(0,1)
> x <- exp(mu_log + x.raw*sigma)

Stan is more imperative than BUGS or JAGS, so
this approach won't work because x is data.

Now that I say that, I realize the reparameterization
is unlikely to help here.

Also keep in mind that the mean of the distribution
lognormal(nu,tau) is exp(nu + tau^2/2). This is
described here:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution

In particular, the variance plays into the mean because
of the skew (log normal, unlike the normal, is not symmetric).

> I'm not quite sure whether the last reparameterization also requires me also to specify the Jacobian of the transform,
> so perhaps someone can comment on this. This Jacobian stuff is really beyond me (I'm not a statistician or
> mathematician). I abandonned the approach altogether when the model went completely berserk. May give it another try
> later, once I have solved the other issues pointed out by Bob.

I feel your pain. When the Stan project was starting,
I thought all the formulas for log normal and inverse gamma
and what not were wrong in Andrew's book because I didn't know
about Jacobians.

There's a fairly gentle intro in the transforms chapter of
the manual. It might help if you're playing with lognormal
models.

- Bob

On Sunday, March 17, 2013 9:46:47 AM UTC+1, Luc Coffeng wrote:
Dear Stan Developers,

First of all, thanks for making my life easier! I really appreciate how the Stan language forces me to properly write up a model. With BUGS, I was always debugging my models for what seems like ages, which is no longer the case with Stan.

I would like to pose a question about non-linear model behaviour. I'm working on a hierarchical model for blood parasite levels in experimentally infected subjects, assuming a log-normal distribution for blood parasite levels. The blood parasites appear in cycles of generations, each cycle being modeled by two scaled normal cdf's (one for the build-up of parasites, another for the disappearing of parasites). To anchor the model, I'm explicitly modeling censored observations, and I assume that all observations up to the first observation above the detection limit are samples of first generation of blood parasites.

data {
  int<lower=1> Nobs;                                // Number of observations;
  int<lower=1> Nind;                                // Number of individuals;
  int<lower=1> Nobs_ind[Nind];                      // Number of observations in each individual;
  int<lower=1> Ncyc;                                // Number of cycles to model;
 
  int<lower=1> N_cens1;                             // Number of censored observations before first positive observation;
  int<lower=1> id_cens1[N_cens1];                   // Individual to which censored observation pertains;
  real<lower=0> time_cens1[N_cens1];                // Time of censored observation;
  real<lower=0> dlimit_cens1[N_cens1];              // Lower detection limit of blood parasite concentrations;
 
  int<lower=1> N_cens2;                             // Number of censored observations after first positive observation;
  int<lower=1> id_cens2[N_cens2];                   // Individual to which censored observation pertains;
  real<lower=0> time_cens2[N_cens2];                // Time of censored observation;
  real<lower=0> dlimit_cens2[N_cens2];              // Lower detection limit of blood parasite concentrations;
 
  int<lower=1> N_firstpos;                          // Number of first positive observations;
  int<lower=1> id_firstpos[N_firstpos];             // Individual to which first positive observation pertains;
  real<lower=0> time_firstpos[N_firstpos];          // Time of first positive observation;
  real<lower=0> pf_ml_firstpos[N_firstpos];         // Value of first positive observation;
 
  int<lower=1> N_cyc1plus;                          // Number of non-censored observations after first positive observation;
  int<lower=1> id_cyc1plus[N_cyc1plus];             // Individual to which non-censored observation after first positive observation pertains;
  real<lower=0> time_cyc1plus[N_cyc1plus];          // Time of non-censored observation after first positive observation;
  real<lower=0> pf_ml_cyc1plus[N_cyc1plus];         // Value of non-censored observation after first positive observation;
 
  real<lower=0> s2;                                 // Standard deviation (within individuals) of time of disappearance of parasites (currently set to zero);
  real<lower=0> s3;                                 // Standard deviation (within individuals) of duration of undetectable parasite form (currentlyset to zero);
  real<lower=0> constant;                           // Small constant to add to modeled parasite blood concentration for numerical stability;
}
parameters {
  real log_T1;                                      // Log average time of appearance of parasites in the population;
  real<lower=5,upper=12> t1[Nind];                  // Average time of appearance of parasites in individuals;
  real<lower=0,upper=10> S_T1;                      // Standard deviation (between individuals) of time of appearance of parasites;
  real<lower=0> s1;                                 // Standard deviation (within individuals) of time of appearance of parasites;
 
  real<lower=0,upper=4> t23;                        // Parasite generation time;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> t2of3;                      // Fraction of parasite generation time spent in detectable form;
 
  real log_M1;                                      // Log average number of parasites per ml blood during first cycle in the population;
  real<lower=0> m1[Nind];                           // Number of parasites per ml during first cycle in individuals;
  real<lower=0,upper=10> S_M1;                      // Standard deviation (between individuals) of average number of parasites per ml during first cycle;
 
  real<lower=0> log_R;                              // Log average number of new parasites per parasite from previous cycle in population;
  real<lower=1> r[Nind];                            // Number of new parasites per ringform from previous cycle in individuals;
  real<lower=0,upper=10> S_R;                       // Standard deviation (between individuals) of log number of new parasites per parasite from previous cycle;
 
  real<lower=0,upper=10> sigma;                     // Standard deviation of measurement error in log-concentration of parasites;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> t2;                                 // Duration of detectable parasite form;
  real<lower=0> t3;                                 // Duration of undetectable parasite form;
  real<lower=1> R;                                    // Average number of parasites per ml blood during first cycle in the population;
 
  t2 <- t23 * t2of3;
  t3 <- t23 * (1 - t2of3);
  R <- exp(log_R);
}
model {
  real PF_ML_CENS1[N_cens1];                        // True value of censored observations before first positives;
  real PF_ML_CENS2[N_cens2,Ncyc];                   // True value of censored observations after first positives;
  real PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[N_firstpos];                  // True value of first positive observations;
  real PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[N_cyc1plus,Ncyc];             // True value of positive observations after the first positive observation;
 
  real log_PF_ML_CENS1[N_cens1];                    // Log true value of censored observations before first positives;
  real log_PF_ML_CENS2[N_cens2];                    // Log true value of censored observations after first positives;
  real log_PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[N_firstpos];              // Log true value of first positive observations;
  real log_PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[N_cyc1plus];              // Log true value of positive observations after the first positive observation;

  t1 ~ lognormal(log_T1,S_T1);
  m1 ~ lognormal(log_M1,S_M1);
  r ~ lognormal(log_R,S_R);   

  for (c in 1:N_cens1) {
    PF_ML_CENS1[c] <- constant +
        m1[id_cens1[c]]
        * (normal_cdf( time_cens1[c],  t1[id_cens1[c]]      , s1 )
        -  normal_cdf( time_cens1[c], (t1[id_cens1[c]] + t2), sqrt(s1*s1 + s2*s2) ));
    log_PF_ML_CENS1[c] <- log(PF_ML_CENS1[c]);
  }
 
  for(cc in 1:N_cens2) {
    for(k in 1:Ncyc) {
      PF_ML_CENS2[cc,k] <- constant +
          m1[id_cens2[cc]] * pow(r[id_cens2[cc]],(k-1))
          * (normal_cdf( time_cens2[cc], (t1[id_cens2[cc]] + (k-1) * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 + (k-1) * s2*s2 + (k-1) * s3*s3) )
          -  normal_cdf( time_cens2[cc], (t1[id_cens2[cc]] +     k * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 +     k * s2*s2 + (k-1) * s3*s3) ));
    }
  log_PF_ML_CENS2[cc] <- log(sum(PF_ML_CENS2[cc]));
  }

  for(f in 1:N_firstpos) {
    PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[f] <- constant +
        m1[id_firstpos[f]]
        * (normal_cdf( time_firstpos[f],  t1[id_firstpos[f]]      , s1 )
        -  normal_cdf( time_firstpos[f], (t1[id_firstpos[f]] + t2), sqrt(s1*s1 + s2*s2) ));
    log_PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[f] <- log(PF_ML_FIRSTPOS[f]);
  }
 
  for(p in 1:N_cyc1plus) {
    for(k in 1:Ncyc) {
      PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[p,k] <- constant +
          m1[id_cyc1plus[p]] * pow(r[id_cyc1plus[p]],(k-1))
          * (normal_cdf( time_cyc1plus[p], (t1[id_cyc1plus[p]] + (k-1) * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 + (k-1) * s2*s2 + (k-1) * s3*s3) )
          -  normal_cdf( time_cyc1plus[p], (t1[id_cyc1plus[p]] +     k * t2 + (k-1) * t3), sqrt(s1*s1 +     k * s2*s2 + (k-1) * s3*s3) ));
    }
  log_PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[p] <- log(sum(PF_ML_CYC1PLUS[p]));
  }

  for (c in 1:N_cens1) {
    lp__ <- lp__ + log(lognormal_cdf(log(dlimit_cens1[c]),log_PF_ML_CENS1[c],sigma));     // Integrate out censored value;
  }
  for (cc in 1:N_cens2) {
    lp__ <- lp__ + log(lognormal_cdf(log(dlimit_cens2[cc]),log_PF_ML_CENS2[cc],sigma));   // Integrate out censored value;
  }
  pf_ml_firstpos ~ lognormal(log_PF_ML_FIRSTPOS,sigma);
  pf_ml_cyc1plus ~ lognormal(log_PF_ML_CYC1PLUS,sigma);
}

My model is compiling nicely, and comes up with very plausible parameter estimates. Also, visually, the model predictions fit the data well (see attached example). However, when looking at the traceplots, it seems that the model sometimes gets 'spontaneously' stuck at a set of parameter values for some hundreds of MC simulations at a time (coinciding with a high lp, and with all of the parameters having plausible values, no zeros or infinities etc). In general, N.eff is very low. Is there a way to get this (or any model) explore local maxima/minima more efficiently? I have tried to leave out the hierarchical components for parameter R (number of new parasites per parasite), which considerably improved mixing of chains (and I haven't noticed the sampler getting stuck when doing this). Still, I'm interested to know whether it is possible to further improve sampling efficiency.

Thanks in advance for any pointers!

Luc

Dear Bob,

I just picked up where I left of in March, hoping that some of the issues of earlier versions of STAN have been resolved. Justed wanted to notify you that in the current version of rstan (1.3.0), truncation and vectorization of the lognormal distribution do work, but not when used at the same time:

TRANSLATING MODEL 'Coffeng2013Malaria' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
  failed to parse Stan model 'Coffeng2013Malaria' with error message:
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=70, column=3

  t1 ~ lognormal(log_T1,S_T1) T[5,12];

^-- here


DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
no matches for function name="lognormal_cdf"
    arg 0 type=real[1]
    arg 1 type=real
    arg 2 type=real

available function signatures for lognormal_cdf:
0.  lognormal_cdf(real, real, real) : real

lower bound in truncation type does not match sampled variate in distribution's type
Parser expecting: "}"

t1 is declared in the parameter block as "real<lower=5,upper=12> t1[Nind]" ); log_T1 and S_T1 are parameters with unknown values, hence I need the truncation of the prior for t1 (because of the non-constant values of log_T1 and S_T1). Specifying a loop for each component of t1 solves the issue (though is somewhat slower).

Best,
Luc

all the distributions, which should make truncated
models faster.

- Bob
